title: A Study of 463,000 People Found That Loneliness Raises Your Risk of Heart Valve Disease by 23 Per Cent. Living Alone Does Not. The Distinction Matters More Than You Think.
excerpt: The largest study of its kind found that feeling lonely — not being socially isolated — independently predicts degenerative valve disease. For a diaspora that prizes stoicism and treats loneliness as weakness, the findings are a clinical alarm bell.
body:
Your grandmother would have called it a broken heart. Cardiologists now call it a modifiable risk factor.

A study published in the *Journal of the American Heart Association* has found that adults who report feeling lonely have a 19 to 23 per cent higher risk of developing degenerative heart valve disease — even after the researchers controlled for age, genetics, smoking, obesity, diet, sleep, and every other traditional cardiovascular risk factor in the book.

The study followed 462,917 adults enrolled in the UK Biobank for nearly 14 years. During that time, more than 11,000 new cases of degenerative valvular heart disease were diagnosed. The researchers separated loneliness — the subjective feeling of missing meaningful connection — from social isolation, the objective state of living alone and having infrequent contact with others. The results were striking.

## The Numbers That Should Worry You

Compared with people who reported minimal loneliness, those with the highest loneliness scores had a 19 per cent higher risk of degenerative valvular heart disease overall, a 21 per cent higher risk of aortic valve stenosis — the dangerous narrowing of the valve that allows blood to leave the heart — and a 23 per cent higher risk of mitral valve regurgitation, where the valve between the heart's left chambers fails to close properly and blood leaks backward.

Social isolation, by contrast, showed no significant association with any form of valve disease. You can live alone and eat dinner by yourself every night and your heart valves will not care. But if you *feel* lonely — if there is a gap between the connections you want and the ones you have — your valves are listening.

"Loneliness is not just an emotion," said Crystal Wiley Cené, a professor of medicine at the University of California, San Diego, and an American Heart Association expert who was not involved in the study. "Chronic loneliness is a stressor for the body that can damage people's health. Patients and health care professionals need to understand the importance of talking about loneliness as a health risk, not a moral failing or sign of weakness."

## Why This Hits the Indian Diaspora Harder

The study's participants were overwhelmingly white British adults. The researchers themselves acknowledged the need for replication in more diverse populations. But the implications for South Asians in the West are hard to ignore.

First-generation Indian immigrants in the US, UK, and Canada face a loneliness profile that is structurally different from the majority population. They leave behind extended family networks — the joint-family system, the colony aunties, the evening walks with neighbours — and replace them with suburban isolation, demanding work schedules, and a cultural script that treats loneliness as a character flaw rather than a medical signal.

Asian Americans already have the lowest rate of anxiety medication use in the country, as a separate study of 29,000 adults recently found. The stigma around admitting emotional distress is well documented. Now add a finding that says feeling lonely — not living alone, not working from home, not being an introvert — independently damages your heart valves, and the gap between what is happening inside South Asian bodies and what South Asians are willing to say out loud becomes a clinical emergency.

The study also found that unhealthy lifestyle behaviours — obesity, smoking, excess alcohol, poor sleep, and physical inactivity — partially explained the relationship between loneliness and valve disease. These are behaviours that tend to cluster in people who feel disconnected: you eat worse, move less, sleep badly, and drink more when you feel nobody would notice or care.

## What You Can Do

The researchers were cautious about causation — this was an observational study, not a clinical trial. But the lead author, Zhaowei Zhu, an associate professor of cardiovascular medicine at The Second Xiangya Hospital in China, said the findings "suggest that addressing loneliness could help delay disease progression, postpone surgical interventions such as valve replacement, and ultimately reduce the long-term clinical and economic burden of valvular heart disease."

For NRIs, the practical implications are straightforward. Talk to your doctor about how you feel, not just what you eat and how much you exercise. If your parents moved to the US decades ago and now live alone in a house that once had three generations in it, their loneliness is not a phase — it is a cardiovascular risk factor. If you moved abroad for work and your social life consists of Slack channels and family WhatsApp groups, the study says your heart is paying attention even if you are not.

Valvular heart disease accounted for more than 440,000 deaths in the US between 1999 and 2020. It is becoming more common as populations age. And now the science says one of its risk factors is something we have been trained to hide.

The study's co-author, Cheng Wei, put it plainly: "Our results suggest that addressing loneliness could help delay disease progression." The first step is admitting you are lonely. For a culture that equates emotional vulnerability with weakness, that may be the hardest prescription to fill.
